passage: On Saturday, Omkar got fifty rupees from his grandmother, and by lunch it was all gone: sweets from the corner shop, then a sticky toffee for me. I am his cousin Tushar and I watched him. He seemed happy. On Sunday there was a fair. He stopped at a stall with a toy car that cost eighty rupees. He held it, turned it over, and set it down. He was quiet for the whole walk home, and for once he did not talk about anything. I could not tell whether he was sad or thinking. The next Saturday, he kept twenty rupees back and put it in a tin.

qa.q: How much money did Omkar get from his grandmother on Saturday?
qa.a: Omkar got fifty rupees from his grandmother.

qa.q: What might Omkar have been feeling as he set the toy car down and walked home quietly?
qa.a: Omkar was probably disappointed and thoughtful, though Tushar could not tell whether he was sad or thinking.

qa.q: What small step did Omkar take the next Saturday?
qa.a: Omkar kept twenty rupees back and put it in a tin, saving toward something bigger.

qa.q: What is it like for Tushar to watch Omkar at the toy stall?
qa.a: Tushar sees a younger cousin learn something without being told, and does not lecture, but cannot be sure what is going on in Omkar's mind.

grounding: Shows a child spending pocket money on sweets at once and later wanting something bigger, then beginning to save.

Friday. Abhinav got thirty rupees from his mother Jaya and bought sweets and a fizzy drink before he reached home. "All gone!" he said, and licked his fingers.
Tuesday. At the shop window he saw a cricket ball for sixty rupees. He stood there so long that the shopkeeper asked if he wanted it. He shook his head, walking off, shoulders low.
Three Fridays later, Abhinav counted coins from an old jar, twenty rupees each week. He put them on the counter and took the ball, holding it in both hands all the way home.

qa.a: Abhinav got thirty rupees from his mother Jaya.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling as he stood at the shop window looking at the cricket ball?
qa.a: Abhinav felt longing and disappointment, since he wanted the ball but had spent his money on sweets.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do that led him to the cricket ball?
qa.a: Abhinav put coins into a jar over three weeks until he had enough to buy it.

qa.q: How might Jaya have felt watching Abhinav save for the ball?
qa.a: Jaya was probably proud and quietly pleased that Abhinav learned to wait for a bigger wish without being told.

grounding: Shows a child spending pocket money on sweets at once and later wanting something bigger, then saving toward the goal.

subtype: Pocket money and spending at once [Actor]
passage: Tarun, nine, got his fifty rupees of pocket money on Saturday morning. The village fair was on Sunday, and his sister Ankita had told him about a spinning top with lights that cost forty rupees. But on Saturday afternoon, the sweets man came down the lane with his cart. Tarun bought jalebis, then a coconut barfi, then a packet of colourful toffees. By evening, the money was gone. On Sunday, at the fair, he stood in front of the spinning top, lights flashing. Ankita had kept her money and bought a small drum. Tarun's eyes filled. On Monday he asked Ankita, "How did you not eat the jalebis?" She shrugged. "I kept thinking about the drum."

qa.q: How much did the spinning top cost?
qa.a: It cost forty rupees.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel in front of the spinning top?
qa.a: He felt sad and full of regret, his eyes filling because his money was gone.

qa.q: What could help Tarun next time he gets pocket money?
qa.a: Keeping a picture of what he wants in mind, like Ankita did with the drum, so the bigger wish can win over the sweets.

qa.q: How does Ankita see her choice?
qa.a: Ankita kept thinking about the drum she wanted, so the jalebis did not tempt her as much.

grounding: Shows a child spending pocket money on sweets at once and feeling the difference when a bigger wish comes along.

subtype: Pocket money and spending at once [Actor]
passage: Tejas, ten, lived in a flat in Chennai and got pocket money every Monday. Every Monday afternoon, he spent it at the shop below: chips, a cola, sticker packets. It felt wonderful for about ten minutes. Then his friend Samir came over with a new cricket bat he had saved up for over two months. Tejas held it and felt a pang of envy. "I want one." His mother said, "What if you kept a little each week in this jar?" She drew a picture of a bat on the jar. The next Monday, Tejas stood outside the shop, jingling coins, torn. He bought one packet of chips and put the rest in the jar. It felt strange, and a bit proud.

qa.q: How long had Samir saved for the bat?
qa.a: Over two months.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he held Samir's bat?
qa.a: He felt a pang of envy and a new wish for something bigger.

qa.q: What did Tejas's mother do that could help him?
qa.a: She gave him a jar with a picture of a bat on it, so the bigger wish stayed in front of him.

qa.q: How might Samir feel about his bat?
qa.a: Samir likely feels proud, having waited two months to buy it.

grounding: Shows a child who spends pocket money at once, then feels the pull of a bigger wish after seeing a friend's saved-for bat.

subtype: Pocket money and spending at once [Actor]
passage:
Tanvir: "Aditi, didn't you get your pocket money yesterday?"
Aditi: "Yes, Papa. I bought ice cream and chips and a sticker book."
Tanvir: "All of it?"
Aditi: "All of it. It was so good."
Tanvir: "And the art set you showed me in the shop window?"
Aditi: (quiet) "I still want it. It's so much money."
Tanvir: "How does it feel, not having it?"
Aditi: "Bad. The ice cream is gone, but I still want the art set."
Tanvir: "What if we cut out a picture of the art set and stick it on your money box?"
Aditi: "So I remember when I want ice cream?"
Tanvir: "Exactly. You decide each week how much goes in."
Aditi: "Can I still have ice cream sometimes?"
Tanvir: "Sometimes. You choose."

qa.q: What did Aditi buy with the pocket money?
qa.a: Ice cream and chips and a sticker book.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel about not having the art set?
qa.a: Aditi feels bad and a little regretful, since the ice cream is gone but the wish remains.

qa.q: What did Tanvir suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: A picture of the art set on the money box, so Aditi remembers the bigger wish when choosing, while still deciding for herself.

qa.q: How does Tanvir approach Aditi's spending?
qa.a: Tanvir stays calm and asks questions, letting Aditi feel the difference directly instead of scolding.

grounding: A dialogue shows a child who spent all the pocket money at once and a parent helping the child feel the pull of a bigger wish.

subtype: Pocket money and spending at once [Actor]
passage: I'm Kunal. Every Sunday Nani gives me twenty rupees. Last month I spent it the same day, every time: an orange ice lolly, a packet of stickers, once a plastic whistle that broke by Tuesday. Then came Sankranti. Akash had saved his for four weeks and bought a big red kite and a whole roll of string. On the terrace everyone was flying theirs. I had nothing, only a racing-car sticker on my water bottle. Akash let me hold his string for a while, but it wasn't the same. That night I told Nani, "I want a kite like Akash's next year." Nani said, "Then we'll make a jar." The jar is on my shelf now, with sixty rupees in it. I look at it more than I looked at lollies.

qa.q: How much money is in Kunal's jar now?
qa.a: Sixty rupees.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel on the terrace at Sankranti?
qa.a: Kunal felt left out and envious, holding Akash's string but knowing it wasn't the same as having a kite.

qa.q: What choice is helping Kunal work towards the kite?
qa.a: Deciding with Nani to keep the Sunday money in a jar for the kite, so the bigger wish can grow instead of going on lollies.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt letting Kunal hold the string?
qa.a: Akash was probably kind and a bit proud of the kite, happy to share it for a while.

grounding: Shows a child who spends pocket money the same day and then wants something bigger, and feels the difference between a wish now and a wish later.
